content: Hey, I need to have a serious conversation with you today. I've been sitting on this for a while, but I think we need to officially retire the working name 'Ginza Trattoria' and commit to something new before we go any further with signage, menus, or any other tangible deliverables. Every time I tell someone the name, I have to immediately follow it up with 'but it's actually in Azabu' — and that's just embarrassing. It kills the energy of a conversation that should be building excitement. A friend of mine who works in hospitality PR actually laughed when I told her the name and then gave her the address. She wasn't being mean about it, but she said, 'Kenta, that's going to confuse your first hundred guests before you've even served them a single plate of pasta.' And honestly, she's right. The 'Ginza Trattoria' name is confusing since the restaurant is in Azabu, not Ginza at all. I need to fix this now, before we get deeper into the branding work. We're at a stage where the signage vendor is following up on me weekly, Aiko is waiting for a revised brief, and the web developer has the domain sitting there doing nothing. Every additional week I spend under the wrong name is a week where someone could encounter the restaurant for the first time and immediately wonder whether I know what I'm doing. That's not the first impression I want to make.

You're absolutely right to address this now, and honestly, I'm glad you're pulling the trigger on it at this stage rather than six months after opening. Your friend's reaction is exactly the kind of first impression you cannot afford to let become a pattern. The name-location mismatch is a real credibility problem — not just a quirk — because Ginza and Azabu carry very different neighborhood identities in Tokyo dining culture. Ginza reads as formal, corporate-lunch, department-store adjacency, the kind of place you go for a business dinner where the bill gets expensed without any conversation about it. Higashi-Azabu reads as intimate, residential, discerning — the kind of neighborhood where people live intentionally and choose their restaurants carefully. Those aren't interchangeable connotations, and a name that points to the wrong neighborhood will actively work against the atmosphere you're trying to build before a single guest has sat down. The good news is that you've caught this before anything permanent has been installed or printed in quantity. The name exists only in documents and digital files right now, which means the cost of changing it is low and the cost of not changing it compounds every day you leave it. So let's treat this as an opportunity rather than a setback. You've been operating under a placeholder, and now it's time to make the real decision. Walk me through what you've been thinking. Do you have any candidate names already in your head, or are you starting completely fresh?

I've been scribbling things down in a notebook for the past few weeks, actually. Let me share where my head is at, because I've gone through several directions and I want to explain why I've ended up where I have. First, I thought about leaning heavily into the northern Italian regional angle — something like 'Osteria del Nord' or 'Trattoria Piemonte.' The cuisine is rooted in Piemonte and Lombardia, so there's a genuine logic to it and it would tell a guest immediately what kind of food to expect. But then I kept running into the same problem: those names feel very generic. When you search 'Osteria del Nord' in any major city, something comes up. There's one in Amsterdam, probably one in Melbourne, almost certainly one in Paris. I don't want to be fighting for SEO territory with a restaurant on the other side of the world, and I don't want guests arriving with expectations shaped by a completely different kitchen. The second direction I explored was incorporating the neighborhood — 'Azabu Cucina,' 'Higashi-Azabu Table,' 'Casa Azabu,' things like that. Those feel more grounded geographically and they at least put us in the right part of the city. But I worry they sound either too casual, like a lunch spot that does reasonable pasta for the nearby office crowd, or too real-estate-brochure, like a developer named a lobby restaurant after the neighborhood to signal that it was premium without actually committing to anything. Neither of those registers is what I'm trying to build. The third direction, and this is the one I keep coming back to, is using my own name. 'Osteria Morishita.' It's clean, it's personal, it signals ownership and personal pride, and there's a long and respected tradition in Italian dining of restaurants bearing the chef-owner's family name. Think of places like Ristorante Cracco in Milan, or Dal Pescatore up in Canneto sull'Oglio. The name doesn't describe the food; it describes the person accountable for it. Am I overthinking the regional direction, or is there a version of it I should explore further before I commit to putting my own name on the door?

You're not overthinking it at all. You've mapped the decision space clearly and the conclusion you keep arriving at is the right one. The regional appellations like 'Osteria del Nord' and 'Trattoria Piemonte' are charming, but they carry a structural limitation: they describe the food, not the place, and they don't build any equity in you as the person behind the restaurant. If you run 'Osteria del Nord' for five years and then want to open a second location or launch a wine import project, the regional name gives you nothing to work with. It's also descriptive rather than distinctive as a trademark, which matters if you ever need to protect it. The neighborhood-based names suffer from a different problem. They anchor you in a specific moment in time, and neighborhoods change. Higashi-Azabu has particular associations right now that could shift meaningfully over the next decade, and 'Higashi-Azabu Table' could read very differently in 2032 than it does today. But 'Osteria Morishita' is strong for reasons I want to state explicitly. First, 'osteria' carries a more personal register than 'trattoria': it implies a place driven by the owner's direct hospitality and personal wine curation, which is precisely the experience you've described from the beginning of this project. Second, your family name is genuinely distinctive in Italian dining globally. There is no significant restaurant called 'Osteria Morishita' anywhere I'm aware of, which means you own that combination the moment you use it publicly. Third, it puts your personal reputation on the door — a signal that this place exists because one person believed in it enough to stake their name on it. My recommendation is clear: go with 'Osteria Morishita.'

Okay. We're doing it. Renaming from 'Ginza Trattoria' to 'Osteria Morishita' — that's the decision, and I'm not revisiting it. I feel genuinely relieved saying it out loud. It just sounds right in a way the old name never did. The working name always felt like something I had typed into a spreadsheet before I had a real answer, and now I have a real answer. Now I need to think about what this means practically, because there are several things in motion that need to be updated. The most immediate one is Aiko Fujimoto. She's a freelance logo designer I've been working with on the visual identity, and she came very highly recommended by another restaurateur I respect, someone who opened a well-regarded kaiseki restaurant in Minami-Aoyama a few years back. Aiko did the full visual identity for that place and the work held up beautifully even after they went through a renovation and refreshed a significant portion of the menu. I sent her the old brief when we were still using 'Ginza Trattoria,' so I obviously need to update everything I've sent her. But I don't want to just fire off a name-change email and call it a brief revision. Before I update that document, I want to make sure I'm giving her a genuinely coherent new direction, not just a new name pasted onto the bones of an old brief that was pointing at the wrong kind of restaurant. What should I be thinking about in terms of visual identity for 'Osteria Morishita' specifically? What are the brand signals we want to send into the world, and how do they differ from what a 'Ginza Trattoria' brief would have implied?

That's exactly the right instinct, and it's an important one to hold onto. Updating Aiko Fujimoto's brief isn't a find-and-replace exercise on the name. The name change reflects a genuine philosophical shift in how you're positioning the restaurant, and that shift needs to run through every element of the visual brief you give her. A brief written for 'Ginza Trattoria' was implicitly pointing toward a Ginza register: formal, polished, the kind of visual language that signals 'respectable establishment in a prestigious address.' A brief for 'Osteria Morishita' in Higashi-Azabu should point somewhere meaningfully different, and the sooner you articulate that difference in precise language, the more productive her concept exploration phase will be. Let me walk you through the layers of brand signal that matter most. Starting with the core emotional register: 'Osteria Morishita' should feel warm, unhurried, and deeply personal. The aesthetic equivalent of being welcomed into someone's home in the Langhe hills, but with the discretion and quiet refinement that Higashi-Azabu guests expect from a serious dining destination. That's a specific tension, and it's a productive one if you name it clearly in the brief. I'd phrase it as something like 'rustic soul, precise execution,' which gives a designer two poles to hold in creative tension rather than a single vague direction. For the color palette, I'd steer you firmly toward earth tones that reference both the northern Italian landscape and the physical world of Italian building and tableware. Specifically, think about terracotta and ivory as your primary anchor colors. Terracotta connects to the fired-clay tradition of Italian ceramics and to the warm ochre of Piemontese stone farmhouses; it's a color you can point to in the real world, which is exactly the kind of grounding that works well for a chef-owner restaurant. Ivory provides the breathing room and lightness that prevents the palette from feeling heavy or nostalgic. Together they read as sophisticated without being cold, and they photograph beautifully in both natural daylight and the warmer candlelight of an evening service, which matters a great deal for the kind of social presence a restaurant at your level needs to maintain. For typography, I'd pair a humanist serif — something with visible calligraphic origins that connects to the handwritten tradition — with a clean, minimal grotesque for secondary and functional text. The serif carries the warmth and the Italian heritage; the grotesque signals that this is a contemporary, thoughtfully edited operation, not a nostalgic theme exercise. The logo itself should almost certainly be typographic rather than illustrative. 'Osteria Morishita' in the right letterforms is more durable and more versatile than any emblem or pictogram you could pair with it, and it scales from exterior signage to a favicon without losing legibility or character.

The terracotta and ivory direction makes a lot of intuitive sense to me, and I think Aiko Fujimoto will respond to it well — looking at her past work, she tends to gravitate toward natural, material-reference palettes rather than abstract or trend-driven color choices. So this plays directly to what she's already good at rather than asking her to work in a register that's unfamiliar to her. I had a fairly detailed call with her last week and she walked me through her working process in some depth. She runs everything in three phases. The first is an initial concept exploration phase where she delivers four to six distinct directions as full mood boards and rough logo sketches, giving me a real range to respond to rather than a single take. The second is a refinement phase where we align on one direction and she develops it fully — finalized logo lockups, a working color system with defined values, and typography specimens showing how the system behaves in real-world applications. The third is a final delivery phase with all production files packaged for handoff, a complete brand guidelines document, and print-ready artwork that can go directly to the signage vendor and the menu printer without any intermediate steps. Her fee for this full scope is 320,000 yen, which includes unlimited revisions within each phase but explicitly does not cover full direction changes between phases. So if I let her invest heavily in a direction during the refinement phase and then decide I want to go back to a different concept from the initial exploration, that becomes a separate negotiation. Given that structure and that constraint, is there anything I absolutely need to nail down in the brief before I hand it off? I don't want to waste one of her concept slots on something I would reject immediately.

A logo design fee of 320,000 yen for a three-phase process with production-ready deliverables and a complete brand guidelines document is genuinely reasonable for a Tokyo-based freelancer working at that level of hospitality experience. You're not overpaying. But you're paying enough that you should go into the brief with real specificity, because the cost of ambiguity here is either a wasted concept slot in phase one or a revision loop that pushes you to the edge of what's covered before you've reached a satisfying result. Here's what I'd make sure is locked down before you hand anything over. First and most obviously, the name. Make sure 'Osteria Morishita' appears clearly at the top of the brief, followed by a single positioning sentence that does the work a journalist's lead paragraph would do: chef-owner-driven northern Italian osteria in Higashi-Azabu, opening in 2025, rooted in the food traditions of Piemonte and Lombardia, with a focus on natural wine and seasonal ingredients from both Italian importers and Japanese producers. That sentence should orient Aiko so thoroughly that she doesn't need to guess at the register. Second, give her the color anchors explicitly and frame them as a constraint rather than as one of many possibilities. Tell her that terracotta and ivory are the primary palette and that you want the initial concept directions to work within or in close dialogue with those colors, rather than opening the floor to completely different palettes in each slot. You'll still get real variation in how those colors are deployed — different proportions, different textures, different typography pairings — but you won't lose a slot to something in deep teal and white that you would have rejected immediately regardless of execution. Third, provide visual references in two clear categories. Positive references: restaurants, hotels, or any other brands whose visual identity you admire, even if they're not Italian or in the food space. What you're communicating is your taste, not your category. Negative references: identities you actively dislike or don't want to be compared to. Negative references are often more useful than positive ones because they reveal where your tolerance ends, which is harder to infer from what you like. Fourth, specify the primary applications in priority order: exterior signage at the restaurant address first, the printed menu second, the website header for osteria-morishita.tokyo third, and business cards fourth. That sequence tells Aiko which formats the logo must perform in before all others, and it informs decisions about line weight, small-size legibility, and whether the design can reproduce cleanly in a single ink color for techniques like blind embossing on a menu cover.

This is exactly what I needed. I feel like I'm going into that brief conversation with Aiko with a real point of view now, rather than just a new name and some vague wishes. I'm going to sit down this weekend and write it properly, not just update the old document but start from scratch with the right framing. One more piece I want to get clarity on today is the web presence, because I think that's something I can start moving on in parallel with the logo work, and I don't want to lose more time on it. I've been meaning to handle the domain situation for a while and I finally got around to it this week. I registered the domain osteria-morishita.tokyo, and I have to say I was genuinely surprised it was still available. I half expected someone to have grabbed it already, either speculatively or because some other business was using a similar name somewhere. The .tokyo TLD feels exactly right for this project. It's specific in a way that .com isn't, it announces place without being redundant with the neighborhood name, and honestly I think it looks elegant on print materials. When I imagine it at the bottom of a menu or in the corner of a business card, it reads as intentional rather than default. Now I need to figure out what we actually build on that domain before the opening, and I want to make sure whatever we put up is aligned with the brand work Aiko Fujimoto is doing rather than getting ahead of it and creating a visual inconsistency we then have to walk back. What's your thinking on the web strategy — specifically the pre-opening phase versus the full post-opening site, and how the timing of the two relates to where we are in the branding process?

Registering osteria-morishita.tokyo was exactly the right move, and the timing was good — these things do get taken, sometimes by domain squatters and sometimes by complete coincidence. You're right that the .tokyo extension works particularly well for a restaurant at this address and with this positioning. It reads as local and deliberate rather than just the path of least resistance, and it prints cleanly on a business card or a menu footer in a way that .com doesn't always achieve. Good call to have it in hand before anything else. On the web strategy: I'd structure this as two clearly separated phases with very different objectives, and the most important thing is not letting the urgency of phase one push you into building something that becomes a liability in phase two. Pre-opening, your site has essentially one job: build genuine anticipation while capturing something of lasting value from interested visitors. Everything else is secondary to that single objective. In practice that means a minimal but carefully designed single-page site, probably live within two to three weeks of receiving Aiko Fujimoto's finalized logo files, that contains the restaurant name and address, a brief statement of what Osteria Morishita is and what it stands for in two or three deliberate sentences, an email signup form with a concrete reason to subscribe, and a target opening window rather than an exact date. On the email incentive: early reservation access is the most effective mechanism I know for a restaurant at your level. The people inclined to follow a restaurant before it opens are exactly the guests you want in the room during your first month, and offering priority booking turns a passive expression of interest into a committed act. That list, built carefully over months before opening, is worth more in terms of reliable first-month revenue than most press coverage. What the pre-opening page should not include: placeholder copy, a countdown clock unless you're within three weeks of a confirmed date, or stock photography. If your own photography isn't ready, use a single well-composed image in the terracotta and ivory palette that suggests the mood without making specific promises about what's on the plate. The goal by opening week is somewhere between four and six hundred email addresses from people who are genuinely invested in the concept. Post-opening, the site expands into a proper destination: the complete menu with sourcing notes, the wine list, a reservations widget, and your background story. But the critical sequencing point is this: don't attempt to build the full post-opening site until Aiko's brand guidelines are finalized. Use the minimal pre-opening page as a disciplined holding pattern. Rushing a full site build before the visual system is settled creates inconsistency that's expensive to undo.

The email list idea is something I genuinely want to build a strategy around, not just acknowledge as a good idea and then let sit. I've watched other restaurant openings in Tokyo fumble the pre-opening period in one of two recognizable ways. The first is going completely dark: no website, no social presence, nothing until the doors open, and then having to do all the audience-building from a standing start at exactly the moment when the kitchen is in its most stressful period and no one on the team has any attention to spare. The second is oversharing: posting every construction photo, every equipment delivery, every staff orientation session, every visit from a tile contractor, as if the documentary of the process is inherently interesting to people who actually just want to know whether the food is going to be worth their time. I don't want to do either. My thinking is that the people who voluntarily sign up for a list before a restaurant has even opened its doors are a self-selecting group of exactly the guests I want in the room. They're curious, they're willing to take a small risk on something they can't fully evaluate yet, and they're almost certainly the kind of people whose dining opinions their social circles actually trust. If I can get even three hundred of the right people on that list by opening week, that is meaningful momentum regardless of what the press coverage looks like. Now, let me make sure I have a clean summary of everything we've decided today, because I want to put together a message to Aiko Fujimoto before the end of the week and I want to make sure it's complete. My read on what we've landed on: one, we are officially renaming from 'Ginza Trattoria' to 'Osteria Morishita'; two, we are updating Aiko Fujimoto's brief to include terracotta and ivory as the primary color anchors, a typographic logo approach, a clear positioning sentence, and the priority hierarchy for primary applications; three, we are building a minimal pre-opening page on the osteria-morishita.tokyo domain once the logo files are ready; and four, we are holding the full site development until the brand guidelines document is delivered. Does that capture everything we covered today? Is there anything I've left out, or anything I should be thinking about that we haven't gotten to?

That summary is accurate and well-structured. You've captured the four key decisions in the right order and with the right emphasis. Let me add a handful of closing notes that I think are worth carrying into your communications this week, because a few things didn't come up in the conversation but are worth building into your planning. On the communication to Aiko Fujimoto: when you send the updated brief, spend a paragraph explaining not just what the new name is but why it changed. Tell her that 'Ginza Trattoria' was always a working placeholder, that the restaurant is located at 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu, and that 'Osteria Morishita' reflects the chef-owner model and the neighborhood register much more precisely. Designers respond better to a client who can articulate the thinking behind a decision than to one who just announces a change — it gives her something to anchor the visual exploration to. On the budget: the 320,000 yen fee covers logo, color system, typography, brand guidelines, and production files. Before you finalize anything, have one direct conversation with Aiko about whether website asset exports are included or billed separately. Specifically ask about web-optimized SVG files, multiple favicon sizes, and social media image templates. These are outputs your web developer will need immediately, and it's far better to have the scope conversation now than when you're under time pressure before launch. On the domain: even while you're waiting for logo files, make sure osteria-morishita.tokyo resolves somewhere. A simple unstyled page with the name and an email signup is significantly better than a domain that returns an error, which reads as abandoned. And one thing you didn't raise but should plan for: a pre-reservation intake process. Even before a formal booking system is in place, a simple form collecting name, party size, and preferred opening-week dates gives committed list subscribers something tangible to do. You can manage thirty or forty requests manually; you cannot manage three hundred that way. Get the proper system configured at least six weeks before opening. Today was a useful session. The decision to move forward as Osteria Morishita is the right one, and the clarity you're bringing to the brief will make the 320,000 yen investment in Aiko Fujimoto's process go much further.
